newsitem.title: INDIA: India needs gold market regulation - RBI.
newsitem.headline: India needs gold market regulation - RBI.

text.p: India needs to regulate its gold market and develop a effective futures market as it liberalises its policy on the precious metal, a senior central bank official said on Saturday.

"As the policy on gold gets liberalised, it would be necessary to regulate the gold market and facilitate the development of a smoothly functioning transparent cash and futures market," Usha Thorat, chief general manager of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), told a gold seminar.
She said there should be well laid down procedures for membership, price fixing, settlement, delivery, centralised clearing and settlement in an exchange and code of conduct for members.
Thorat said the forward market in gold was not new to India.

"In the aftermath of World War One, there existed an active gold and silver market in India -- both physical and financial -- and gold and silver options and futures were actively traded in the Bombay Bullion Exchange," she said.

A RBI committee on capital account convertibility, headed by S.S. Tarapore, had suggested in June that government and RBI should take steps to develop a well regulated market in India for gold and gold derivatives including forward trading in 1998/99 (April-March).

A government committee in September 1994 had recommended introduction of forward trading in 17 commodities including silver but not gold. It had said that forward trading in gold should be considered after watching the performance of forward trading in silver.

Thorat said an efficient futures exchange should have standardised contracts, reliable clearing and settlement systems, provide cash, futures and options contract and allow both residents and non-residents to operate in the market.
She said an efficient and freely tradable exchange in India could attract business from Southeast Asia, Australia and the Middle East due to its time zone position.

"It will also bring in particiaption from the major market centres of Zurich, London and New York," she said. "There are tremendous possibilities for Bombay to develop as a major financial market in gold."

Thorat said the gold liberalisation policy as suggested by the Tarapore committee should be seen along with the development of the financial products related to gold and the integration of the other financial markets such as money, securities, forex and capital markets.
